summary: Extend the existing highest-weight roadmap by zero-inclusive sl2 triples, their nilpotent adjoint orbits and increasing representation filtrations. Prove recognition using classical standard and half-spin modules and independently certified exceptional adjoint profiles. Construct geometric weight patterns and prove that they determine the positive real part of a complex semisimple parameter. The integral completion and category-O briefs have independent successor owners, recorded under restructure.

nodes.title: Jordan decomposition and the reduction to distinguished nilpotents
nodes.statement: For semisimple L, the Jordan decomposition ad(x)=S+N comes from unique commuting x_s,x_n∈L. If [x,e]=0 or e is an ad(x)-eigenvector, x_s and x_n preserve that condition with the corresponding semisimple eigenvalue and zero nilpotent contribution. For nonzero semisimple s, L^s is reductive with proper semisimple derived algebra; a nilpotent e∈L^s lies in [L^s,L^s].
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
L is a finite-dimensional semisimple K-Lie algebra (equivalently, in this setting, its Killing form is nondegenerate).
proofSteps: Use nondegenerate Killing form to identify inner derivations; the semisimple/nilpotent Jordan parts of a derivation are derivations (check the generalized-eigenspace bracket rule). Thus their inner elements are x_s,x_n.
Place s in a Cartan via maximal torus structure. Roots vanishing on s give the derived semisimple algebra of its centralizer, with the complementary toral center.

In the centralizer, any nonzero component in that toral center is semisimple, so nilpotence forces that component to vanish. A nonzero semisimple s cannot be central in L, so the derived centralizer has smaller dimension.

nodes.title: Jacobson–Morozov theorem
nodes.statement: Every e∈N(L) extends to an adapted triple (h,e,f). Conversely e and f in every adapted triple are ad-nilpotent, and ad(h) is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues. The zero e has only the zero triple.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
L is a finite-dimensional semisimple K-Lie algebra (equivalently, in this setting, its Killing form is nondegenerate).
proofSteps: Induct on dim L. If L^e contains a nonzero semisimple element, apply the Jordan-centralizer reduction and induction in its derived algebra.
In the remaining case every element of L^e is ad-nilpotent. The Killing pairing of e with L^e vanishes, so e lies in im(ad e); choose h with [h,e]=2e and replace h by its semisimple part.

Apply pinned Engel to the centralizer acting faithfully on L, so it is nilpotent and Kh+L^e is solvable. The solvable algebra Kh+L^e acts triangularly by Lie’s theorem; operators from L^e are strictly triangular. Thus tr(ad h·ad x)=0 for x∈L^e, giving h∈im(ad e). Project a preimage f to the ad(h)-eigenspace −2 to obtain [e,f]=h.

The resulting sl2 action on L has nilpotent raising/lowering operators and diagonalizable integral h by pinned sl2 theory. Each argument is algebraic over K; no analytic integration or complex-field transfer is used.

nodes.title: Algebraic integration of a triple and inner invariance
nodes.statement: An adapted triple determines a rational homomorphism SL2,K→G with differential E↦e,F↦f,H↦h; the zero triple gives the trivial homomorphism. In every finite L-module, any Ad(g) twist is isomorphic to the original module. In particular the triple restricted characters are invariant under simultaneous Ad(G(K))-conjugation.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
L is a finite-dimensional semisimple K-Lie algebra (equivalently, in this setting, its Killing form is nondegenerate).
G is a connected semisimple algebraic K-group with a specified identification Lie(G)≅L; its action is Ad(G(K)), equivalently that of the adjoint form.
M is a finite-dimensional K-Lie module for L; representations mean Lie modules, including those not descending to a chosen non-simply-connected G.
proofSteps: Embed G as a closed subgroup of GL(V) using ReductiveGroups Layer 1. Decompose the restricted sl2-module V into standard modules and integrate their explicit polynomial SL2 actions.

Check the two unipotent one-parameter subgroups lie in G: for a nilpotent X in Lie(G), the finite polynomial exp(tX) preserves the defining ideal. The left-invariant derivation attached to X preserves that ideal, so all Taylor coefficients of each defining function along exp(tX) vanish; factorials are invertible. The upper and lower unipotent subgroups generate SL2, so the integrated map has image in G.

For inner invariance it suffices, by root subgroups and Bruhat, to handle the simple-root SL2 subgroups of G. In any finite L-module their raising/lowering operators are nilpotent by pinned sl2 decomposition; their finite exponentials implement the adjoint twist. Multiply these intertwiners.
All identities are finite polynomial identities over K. The proof does not assume that an arbitrary L-module descends to the selected group G.

nodes.title: Kostant conjugacy for a fixed nilpotent
nodes.statement: For adapted triples (h,e,f) and (h′,e,f′), there is u∈Z_G(e)(K) simultaneously carrying h to h′ and f to f′. Consequently the map from adapted-triple orbits to nilpotent orbits is a bijection.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
L is a finite-dimensional semisimple K-Lie algebra (equivalently, in this setting, its Killing form is nondegenerate).
G is a connected semisimple algebraic K-group with a specified identification Lie(G)≅L; its action is Ad(G(K)), equivalently that of the adjoint form.
proofSteps: For e=0 use the zero branch. Otherwise decompose L under the first triple. L^e has nonnegative h-weights and u=L^e∩[L,e] is precisely its positive-weight part.

The difference h′−h belongs to u. Successively remove its lowest positive-weight component using exp(ad x) for x in that component, dividing by its nonzero weight. Higher commutators raise degree, so the process terminates. Each factor comes from an element of Z_G(e)(K) by triple integration applied to the nilpotent x.
After matching h, the difference of the f entries lies both in L^e and in h-weight −2, so vanishes. Combine this fiber transitivity with Jacobson–Morozov and equivariance.

nodes.title: Conjugacy from the neutral element
nodes.statement: Two adapted triples in L are Ad(G(K))-conjugate iff their neutral elements h,h′ are Ad(G(K))-conjugate. Thus dominant characteristic elements classify triple orbits.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

proofSteps: Reduce to h=h′; zero is immediate. Let L_j be its integer eigenspaces. The map ad(e):L_0→L_2 is surjective by sl2 decomposition, so the Z_G(h)^0-orbit of e is open in the affine space L_2.

The same holds for e′. Characteristic zero ensures separability for the orbit tangent calculation. Two open orbits in irreducible L_2 intersect, and hence coincide. After matching e, f is unique because L^e has no negative h-weights.

nodes.statement: There is a natural K-linear isomorphism gr_i W=W_i/W_(i−1)≅M_i, induced by the eigenspace inclusion. Write d_i=dim gr_i W. Thus equal cumulative dimension functions, equal graded dimension functions, and isomorphic restricted sl2 modules are equivalent.

The comparisons preserve associativity, symmetry, unit and evaluation maps.

nodes.title: Classical triples and partitions with invariant forms
nodes.statement: For L=sl(V), so(V,B) or sp(V,B), the restricted standard module decomposes as ⊕_{n≥0}V(n)⊗U_n, so e has Jordan blocks of size n+1 with multiplicity dim U_n. In type A all partitions of dim V occur. For orthogonal B, each even block size has even multiplicity; for alternating B, each odd block size has even multiplicity. These partitions classify the GL/SL, O, or Sp triple orbits, respectively. For SO(2r), an O-orbit splits into two SO-orbits exactly when its partition is very even (every block size even and each multiplicity even); otherwise it remains one orbit.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
V is finite-dimensional; in orthogonal and symplectic cases B is nondegenerate and respectively symmetric or alternating; the classical semisimple rank hypotheses exclude abelian so2.
proofSteps: The standard V(n) has one Jordan block of size n+1 for E. Its invariant bilinear form is unique up to scalar and is symmetric for even n and alternating for odd n (solve the E,F recurrence in the standard weight basis).

The B-pairing between distinct isotypic summands vanishes by sl2 irreducibility. On V(n)⊗U_n it is the tensor product of that standard invariant form and a nondegenerate form on U_n. Over K, such forms are classified by dimension; alternating multiplicity forms have even dimension. This proves existence and O/Sp uniqueness without importing a book classification table.

In the orthogonal centralizer a symmetric multiplicity factor has an element of determinant −1, whose determinant on V(n)⊗U_n is (−1)^(n+1). Such a factor exists exactly when some odd block size occurs. If all block sizes are even, every orthogonal centralizer element has determinant +1, and index two gives the split. In type A, adjust a GL conjugator to determinant one by a scalar, using algebraic closedness.

sources.match: The classical argument identifies block dimensions with restricted sl2 summands and isolates very-even splitting. The present proof spells out invariant forms instead of treating the cited inaccessible book as read.

nodes.statement: For a very-even partition in so(2r), r is even. Choose ascending positive odd neutral coordinates 0<a1≤…≤ar and simple roots ±ε1+ε2, ε3−ε2,…,εr−ε_(r−1). The two dominant characteristics are (a1,a2,…,ar) and (−a1,a2,…,ar). In the fixed Lie half-spin module S+ whose weights are half-sign vectors with an even number of minus signs, their largest nonzero graded weights are A=½Σa_j and A−a1. Thus their filtration dimension functions differ.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
L is split so(2r), r≥4, and the partition is very even.
proofSteps: Over the algebraic closure, construct the half-spin highest-weight Lie module L(½Σ ε_j) from highest-weight classification. Compute its weights by the minuscule D_r Weyl orbit: the even-minus half-sign vectors. For K=ℂ compare this with the exterior-algebra half-spin construction supplied by SpinRepresentations Layer 5.

The two orthogonal orbit branches differ by changing exactly one coordinate sign. Maximizing over the even-minus sign vectors gives A for the all-positive point; after the first sign change parity requires losing at least a1, and changing the first sign achieves it.
Use graded comparison to pass from differing maximal graded weight to differing cumulative functions. This is a Lie representation (or a representation of Spin), not a claim of descent to SO.

nodes.statement: In a classical simple L, equal W_i dimensions in the standard module determine the adapted triple orbit, except for a very-even pair in type D. In type D adjoining one fixed half-spin highest-weight Lie module to the test family determines the orbit. Hence equality for every finite L-module implies inner conjugacy.

nodes.statement: Conjugate an adapted triple so that h lies in a fixed dominant Cartan chamber. Its simple-root labels a_i=α_i(h) are integers in {0,1,2}, and a is fixed by opposition −w0. For its adjoint grading d_m=dim L_m, d_m=d_(−m) and d_m≥d_(m+2) for every integer m≥0.

proofSteps: Use triple integration to put h in a maximal torus and then in the dominant chamber; integral eigenvalues give nonnegative integral labels.

For a simple root α with α(h)>2, the lowering f kills its root vector: f has degree −2 and its negative-root components cannot subtract a positive root from the simple α to leave a root of positive degree. But lowering is injective in positive weights in every sl2 summand. This contradiction gives the upper bound 2.

nodes.statement: For exceptional type T, let Φ_T be the finite root set in its Bourbaki simple-root lattice Z^r. For a∈Z^r define D_T(a)_m=r·δ_(m,0)+#{c∈Φ_T : Σ_i c_i a_i=m}. Identify each root space with a one-dimensional adjoint eigenspace and the Cartan with its r-dimensional zero-weight summand.

nodes.statement: If L is simple exceptional and two adapted triples have equal adjoint graded multiplicities (equivalently equal W_i dimensions on L for every i), then the triples are Ad(G(K))-conjugate. Thus the adjoint module alone is a test family in every exceptional type, including E6 and E7.

nodes.title: Conjugacy recognition from all representation filtrations
nodes.statement: For two adapted triples t,t′ in semisimple L, the following are equivalent: (1) simultaneous Ad(G(K))-conjugacy; (2) for every finite-dimensional L-module M and i∈Z, dim W_i^t(M)=dim W_i^t′(M); (3) for every such M their restricted sl2 modules are isomorphic. It suffices in (2) to test the pullbacks of the classical standard modules, one chosen Lie half-spin per type-D factor, and the adjoint module of each exceptional factor.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
L is a finite-dimensional semisimple K-Lie algebra (equivalently, in this setting, its Killing form is nondegenerate).
G is a connected semisimple algebraic K-group with a specified identification Lie(G)≅L; its action is Ad(G(K)), equivalently that of the adjoint form.
proofSteps: Use complete reducibility of the adjoint module to decompose L as a finite direct sum of simple ideals; the connected adjoint group is the product of the corresponding adjoint groups. This is a fixed-factor decomposition, so no outer permutation of isomorphic factors is allowed.

Pull back each finite module of one factor along its projection, making the other ideals act trivially. The global dimension hypothesis then yields that factor’s classical or exceptional recognition hypothesis.

Take the product of the factor conjugators and lift it to G(K) through its central isogeny to the adjoint form. Conversely inner invariance identifies restrictions; graded comparison identifies (2) and (3). Treat the empty product L=0 by the zero triple.

nodes.title: Half-integrality on a root-lattice coset
nodes.statement: Let X be an abelian group, Q⊆X the subgroup generated by a finite set of simple roots, ν:X→R an additive functional, and λ∈X. If ν(Q)⊆½Z, then ν(μ)∈½Z iff ν(λ)∈½Z for every μ∈λ+Q. More generally the same assertion holds with any additive subgroup of R in place of ½Z. Membership in ½Z means 2ν(x) is an integer.
hypotheses: X is the actual chosen weight lattice, or X*(T) when applying the result to algebraic G-representations; do not identify them across isogenies.
proofSteps: Express μ−λ as an integer combination of simple roots. Additive subgroup closure gives ν(μ)−ν(λ)∈½Z.
Use subgroup closure under addition and subtraction for the two implications.

sources.match: Every module weight differs from its highest weight by the root lattice; the algebraic coset argument is isolated here.

acceptance: For A1 with α=2ω and ν(α)=1/2, ν(ω)=1/4, so the standard highest-weight module does not have half-integral values; the adjoint highest weight α does.

nodes.title: The highest-weight half-integrality test
nodes.statement: For L semisimple, fix a root base and real linear functional ν on its real weight space. Assume ν(α_i)∈½Z for every simple root. For any dominant integral highest weight λ and its finite irreducible L(λ), every weight μ of L(λ) has ν(μ)∈½Z iff ν(λ)∈½Z. The statement also applies to algebraic G-representations using their genuine character lattice; no dominance of ν is required.
hypotheses: K is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
L is a finite-dimensional semisimple K-Lie algebra (equivalently, in this setting, its Killing form is nondegenerate).
ν is a real functional on the abstract weight lattice tensored with R, not an ordering of elements of K.
proofSteps: Highest-weight theory places every occurring μ in λ+Q and guarantees that λ itself occurs.
Apply the coset lemma in one direction; use occurrence of λ in the other.

For an irreducible algebraic G-module in characteristic zero, differentiation stays irreducible: a Lie-stable subspace is a sum of Cartan weight spaces and hence T-stable, while the root subgroups act by finite exponentials of their derivatives and preserve it. Torus and root-subgroup generation makes it G-stable. Distinct algebraic torus characters have distinct derivatives in characteristic zero. Apply the Lie result with the module’s actual torus weights.

nodes.title: Geometric weight patterns
nodes.statement: Fix q>1 real. For a finite-dimensional complex space V and a semisimple invertible operator A such that every eigenvalue has modulus q^(i/2) for some i∈Z, define n_A:Z→N by the algebraic multiplicity of eigenvalues of modulus q^(i/2). It has finite support and total dim V. For a semisimple s∈G(C) geometric in every finite algebraic representation τ, the representation-indexed weight pattern is (τ,i)↦n_(τ(s))(i). Isomorphic representations have the same function.
hypotheses: The modulus uses the usual complex absolute value; q is fixed and strictly greater than 1.
G is a connected complex semisimple algebraic group; τ is finite-dimensional and algebraic.
proofSteps: The map i↦q^(i/2) is injective. Group eigenvalues by their absolute values; geometricity ensures that every eigenvalue is counted once.
For semisimple A its algebraic eigenspace dimensions equal its eigenvalue multiplicities. Use this comparison rather than defining a new generalized-eigenspace theory.

nodes.title: Positive real part in a complex torus
nodes.statement: For a complex algebraic torus T with character lattice X, let T_pos=Hom(X,R_(>0))⊆T(C). For s∈T(C), define r(s) by χ(r(s))=|χ(s)| for every χ∈X, and u(s)=s/r(s), whose character values have modulus one. Weyl automorphisms commute with absolute value on characters. Maximal-torus conjugacy and semisimple conjugacy in a fixed torus therefore make its Weyl orbit independent of choices.
In an algebraic representation, the eigenvalues of τ(r(s)) are the moduli of the T-weight values at s, counted with the same weight multiplicities.

nodes.title: Algebraic characters with a prescribed leading weight
nodes.statement: Let G be connected complex semisimple, T a maximal torus, and choose positive roots. For every dominant λ in the actual lattice X*(T), there exists a finite algebraic G-module V_λ whose formal character is the orbit sum of λ plus an integer combination of orbit sums of strictly lower dominant weights. The λ-weight has multiplicity one, all other weights lie in λ minus the positive-root monoid, and the character is W-invariant. This existence statement is the group-to-character bridge; it does not assume that every finite Lie module descends to G.
hypotheses: Use opposite Borels B−=TU− and B+=TU+ and the chosen character lattice, without replacing it by the simply connected weight lattice.
proofSteps: In the native coordinate Hopf algebra O(G), consider regular functions satisfying f(gb)=λ(b)^(-1)f(g) for b∈B−. Define f_λ on the dense open cell U+TU− by f_λ(u+tu−)=λ(t)^(-1). This is an auxiliary subspace of O(G), not a new induced-representation carrier.

Extend f_λ over each simple-reflection translate of the open cell. The SL2 root-subgroup identity makes the extra coordinate occur with exponent ⟨λ,α∨⟩≥0. Bruhat dimensions show that the omitted cells have codimension at least two. Extension across that remainder can be proved on translates of U+TU−: each chart is affine space times a torus, so its coordinate algebra is a Laurent polynomial UFD. A reduced denominator would have an irreducible divisor meeting the already covered open set, a contradiction. Thus the rational function is regular on every chart and glues globally; this argument does not assume an unprovided general Hartogs theorem.

Use local finiteness of the coordinate comodule to take the finite-dimensional G-span V_λ of f_λ. Restriction to the open cell is injective. Its right-B−-equivariance identifies that restriction with polynomial functions on U+ times λ(t)^(-1); under left T-translation the coordinate weights subtract positive roots. Hence all weights are ≤λ and its λ-weight space consists of constants, of dimension one. The normalizer of T makes the character W-invariant, yielding the claimed orbit-sum triangularity.

Every finite algebraic module has a finite composition series, and traces and formal characters add in short exact sequences. Consequently the triangular characters of V_λ lie in the span of simple algebraic characters. No assertion of Lie-module descent, Borel–Weil cohomology, or a positive-characteristic Weyl formula is needed.

sources.locator: Part II, Proposition II.2.2 p.176, Proposition II.2.6 pp.178–179 and Corollary II.2.7 p.179
sources.match: The existence proof extends a regular semi-invariant by simple-root SL2 identities. Only the finite coordinate-comodule span and its leading weight are needed here.

nodes.title: Characters separate Weyl orbits in a torus
nodes.statement: Let G be connected complex semisimple, T a maximal torus, W its Weyl group, and x,y∈T(C). If tr τ(x)=tr τ(y) for every irreducible finite algebraic G-representation τ, then x and y are W-conjugate. The highest weights range over the dominant weights in X*(T), so the statement holds for any isogeny form.
hypotheses: Use algebraic representations, not arbitrary abstract representations of G(C).
proofSteps: The preceding existence theorem gives triangular algebraic characters for every dominant weight in X*(T). Dominance induction expresses every W-orbit sum as a linear combination of these characters. A finite composition series expresses each of their characters as a sum of simple algebraic characters, so the simple algebraic characters span C[X*(T)]^W.

Invariant Laurent polynomials separate finite W-orbits: if the two orbits are disjoint, choose a Laurent polynomial taking 0 on one finite orbit and 1 on the other by interpolation of the finitely many distinct torus points. Average its W-translates and divide by |W|.
Equal irreducible characters therefore force equal invariant functions and exclude disjoint orbits. This finite-group argument requires no general GIT quotient theorem.

sources.match: Triangular algebraic characters span the invariant character algebra.
The proof invokes determination of the positive parameter by all representation characters; the invariant-character argument makes this input explicit.

acceptance: For PGL2 only even SL2 highest weights are legal; nevertheless their characters separate PGL2 torus Weyl orbits.

nodes.title: Recognition of the positive real part
nodes.statement: Fix q>1. It suffices to compare patterns on irreducibles. No conjugacy of s and s′ themselves is asserted.
hypotheses: G is connected complex semisimple; positive parts and patterns use the preceding definitions.
proofSteps: For each irreducible τ, compute tr τ(r(s))=Σ_i n_(τ(s))(i)·q^(i/2), using the positive-part eigenvalue comparison. The equal-pattern hypothesis makes these traces equal for s and s′.
Apply character separation in the fixed torus. Direct-sum additivity explains why irreducibles suffice.

sources.match: All geometric weight patterns determine the real part up to Weyl action.

acceptance: The compact-phase SL2 example in the pattern tests is allowed and shows why the conclusion concerns only positive real parts.

Weights of L(λ) lie in λ plus the root lattice and λ occurs. Import ordinary PBW/Verma theory rather than planning it here.

Finite-dimensional irreducibles for every dominant integral Lie weight, including D_r half-spin; this is Lie-module classification, not a claim that these modules all descend to an algebraic group. The narrow algebraic-character existence bridge is proved in N5.
